profile.reading:
The Goldman Sachs facility at 755 U.S. Route 202 in Bridgewater Township, Somerset County, New Jersey sits within a corporate real estate footprint the bank operates for internal, non-marketed IT infrastructure -- distinct from the leased colocation facilities that increasingly cluster along this stretch of central New Jersey. Goldman Sachs does not publish a facility page, floor plan, or capacity sheet for this address, consistent with how the firm generally treats its owned infrastructure: as private operational real estate supporting trading, risk, and enterprise systems rather than a product marketed to outside tenants.

Even so, public construction-industry records fill in real detail. Electrical contractors JW Carrigan and Scholes Electric & Communications both list a project called Goldman Sachs DC2 in Bridgewater, New Jersey in their published data-center portfolios, describing new data center infrastructure built out over a 10-month schedule on a 275,000-square-foot facility. Per those contractor case studies, the DC2 build included 26kV and 15kV electrical feeders, twenty-two UPS modules, and seven 2.2-megawatt, 15kV standby generators tied into 26kV utility service -- power infrastructure consistent with a large enterprise data hall, with over 15 megawatts of standby generation alone, though Goldman Sachs itself has not confirmed these figures or attributed them publicly to this specific address. The 'DC2' designation implies a companion facility (DC1) elsewhere in Goldman's real estate portfolio, though this profile has not independently located or confirmed that sister site.

The Bridgewater location sits within Somerset County's U.S. Route 202/206 corridor, an area with a mix of corporate campuses and, increasingly, third-party data center development; Bridgewater Township's planning board has more recently taken up a dedicated data-center zoning ordinance (Ordinance 26-15) setting standards for renewable-energy offsets and cooling-system review on future hyperscale and data-center redevelopment applications, reflecting rising local interest in the sector, though that ordinance targets new redevelopment-plan applications rather than existing corporate sites like this one.

In short: this is very likely a substantial enterprise data center run for Goldman Sachs's own internal use, evidenced by contractor-side construction records showing tens of millions of dollars in electrical and standby-power infrastructure and a quarter-million square feet of built space, even though neither Goldman Sachs nor any government filing has published an official capacity, tenancy, or certification statement for the site -- typical for a bank's proprietary infrastructure, which is deliberately kept out of public view for both competitive and security reasons.
